title: Wolff on the challenge of unlocking Russell’s potential
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has explained how Mercedes need to work with George Russell to "unleash his potential” after he endured another setback in the title fight in Madrid, with team mate Kimi Antonelli outscoring him once again.

Russell was open about his struggles with tyre degradation over the weekend at the new circuit, which contributed to him missing out on the fight for pole position and settling for sixth place in Qualifying.

From there, the team executed a two-stop strategy to switch the Briton onto medium tyres under the Virtual Safety Car, and back to a second set of hards later in the race. Russell questioned the decision at first, but later admitted that it didn’t significantly impact his final result of P5.

Although he finished close behind Charles Leclerc, there was a gap of nearly 30s to race winner Antonelli, who has subsequently increased his lead over Russell to 81 points in the Drivers’ Championship.

“You can see the pace he had towards the end when he was catching Leclerc,” Wolff said. “You know that he was fastest out on track but after the tyre changes, the pace wasn't there and I just don't know where it is. We have to analyse it because clearly it's in him, it's in the car and we just have to unlock it.

“When it comes to George, you can have good races, bad races, good years and bad years, but we're talking about the driver that has won everything that you could have potentially won before.

“Every single karting championship, Formula 3 in his rookie year, Formula 2 in his rookie year, went into the Williams. I mean, we're talking about a top driver.

“We need to find out what it is for him to be able to unleash that potential, and of course there's the psychological side. If you have a run like him this year you're taking a beating but the great ones, they recover and I think that George has all he needs to fight for championships.”

With Antonelli’s significant advantage over Russell and rivals like Lewis Hamilton, who now sits 101 points adrift following his retirement from the Spanish Grand Prix, Mercedes are in a comfortable position heading into the remaining rounds.

Russell effectively ruled himself out of the championship battle after Sunday’s result, but Wolff was adamant that the situation can change at any given moment, especially with nine rounds to go.

“It's a mechanical sport,” the Team Principal explained. “You can DNF, you can crash out and it happens two times in a row and then suddenly what looked like a nice buffer is not anymore because you have six races to go.

“So in my opinion, we just need to ignore the points until it is mathematically not realistic anymore, or not real anymore for them to win, and until then just concentrate on each and every weekend, try to bring your best game.

“2027 [development] started a while ago already, long before the summer. We switched resources into the next year and that continues as per the plan, independent of where we're standing in the championship.”

title: Piastri assesses his ‘painful’ Spanish GP in Madrid
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri had a race to forget in Madrid after a first lap incident derailed his afternoon on a day where Lando Norris showed the McLaren had the pace to fight for the win.

The Australian finished down in eighth place, behind the Alpine of Franco Colapinto, and while the unlucky timing of the Virtual Safety Car prevented his team mate from fighting for the win, Piastri had his own slice of misfortune.

He picked up damage to his front wing after first lap contact with George Russell’s Mercedes, with the Australian left nowhere to go as the Mercedes ducked across the track towards the barriers. That left him with aero damage in the form of a broken end-plate and short on downforce, something the team could only mitigate but not fully fix at his one and only pit stop.

And having started on the hard tyres, the timing of the early Virtual Safety Car also proved problematic for the 25-year-old.

“It was pretty painful obviously, from Lap 1," he assessed afterwards. "Yeah, not much I really could have done from there.

"The timing for the VSC was certainly not ideal for us, [stayed] on the hard and it was just a difficult afternoon."

Having opted not to stop under the VSC, Piastri ran a long opening stint in the hopes of a later VSC, Safety Car or red flag moment. But no more incidents came, leaving him to make a pit stop under full racing conditions.

The time lost meant he came out in traffic and, while he pulled off one of the few overtakes on Sunday, picking off Arvid Lindblad, Piastri could not find a way past the Alpine of Colapinto late on.

To trace back the difficulties Piastri faced, you have to look to Qualifying where he needed an extra set of softs to guarantee he made it through Q2. That left him as the only front runner to have a used set of the C4 tyre for his first run in Q3.

On his second run on the new tyres, where balance would have been different to the used set, he made a mistake early in his lap and from there, could only qualify seventh.

That left him starting in the midst of the pack, something always fraught with danger as all the cars barrel down into Turn 1 on a narrow street track.

“It was mostly the end of Qualifying and then Lap 1 obviously was far from ideal, having damage for the whole race,” he explained.

“It was tough like that, but today we just tried to learn as much as we could to try and get more out of the car and the way I drive it. Hopefully we’ve learned a few things for the rest of the year.”

Piastri has two podiums to show for his 2026 season, the last of which came in Miami, and one top-three finish in a Sprint. His team mate has five rostrums, including two victories, a Sprint win, three other Sprint top-three finishes, three pole positions and a Sprint pole.

The contrast between their two seasons is stark, and is further highlighted in the Championship where Norris has amassed 66 more points than his team mate.

Piastri will be hoping his luck changes soon, and he has a chance to set things right next time out in Azerbaijan. Last year it was the event that saw his championship hopes dealt their first big blow after an early DNF - something he will want to atone for when the F1 paddock reconvenes in Baku in two weeks' time.

title: Why Vasseur believes Ferrari had the pace to win in Madrid
excerpt:
Fred Vasseur was confident that Charles Leclerc could’ve won the Spanish Grand Prix if an incident had disrupted the latter stages of the race, with the Ferrari Team Principal believing that “the potential is there” for the team.

Leclerc qualified fifth and gained an early position from the retirement of his team mate Lewis Hamilton, but unlike those around him, he and the team opted not to pit for fresh tyres when the Virtual Safety Car was deployed.

As a result, he inherited the lead and maintained a consistent gap to Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli, with Ferrari hoping that the race would see a red flag or Safety Car to give Leclerc what would essentially be a free pit stop.

Unfortunately, that didn’t materialise and he was finally called in after spending nearly 50 laps on the hard compound, dropping him out of podium contention. He eventually crossed the line 29.116s behind Antonelli and narrowly held off George Russell for P4.

“You see that you always have positives and negatives, it doesn't matter the weekend,” Vasseur said. “The pace of Charles in the race was more than good – we did a stint of 49 laps I think with the hard and the pace was still there.

“All the teams did the same with one car on softs or mediums and another one on hards to cover all the options. He was leading the group of [drivers on] hards and I think with a second incident, a red flag, it was the win.

“A Safety Car, it would have been P2, P3. It's more a strategy than something else and on his side, the pace was good. It's the only thing that we can do on Sunday. If we missed something, it's more yesterday [in Qualifying]. Today I think we did what we had to do – we took the risks we had to take and the pace is the pace that we need to have.”

While Leclerc was able to demonstrate Ferrari’s strength in race trim, Hamilton only lasted a short time before a brake issue forced him to retire the car, marking his first DNF of the season.

The Briton enjoyed a fantastic launch to instantly challenge Max Verstappen for P3, with the Dutchman offering him the position after he cut the first corner. However, Hamilton quickly began to drop back as he reported that the brake pedal was going long and he couldn’t stop the car.

He did manage to make it safely back to the garage, where he was left to rue the missed opportunity, telling Sky Sports F1: “I think we had the car to fight for a win today, and unfortunately it just didn't work out.”

Asked whether the problem was caused by a small brush with the wall, Vasseur replied: “Obviously I don't know, because they were working on the car when I left. The pedal was long on the end of Lap 1, I think, and we tried to fix it from the pit wall, and then it happened again a couple of corners later, and at this kind of track it makes no sense to take a crazy risk.

“There were still 56 [laps to go]. The first time it happened was from Lap 2 and it was too risky.”

title: Honda announce changes to leadership of power unit programme
excerpt:
Honda have announced that they will make changes to the leadership of their Formula 1 power unit development programme.

Monday's announcement confirmed that Yoichiro Fukao, currently serving as Deputy Leader of the F1 Project, would take over the role of Large Project Leader from October 1, succeeding Tetsushi Kakuda who has led the programme to date.

"This organisational change is a planned transition designed to ensure the reliable transfer of technical expertise to the next generation of engineers," read a statement from Honda.

"Following the introduction of the new regulations in 2026, and with further regulatory changes expected from 2027 onwards, Honda aims to establish a robust development framework and deliver a highly competitive PU by transitioning to the new structure at an early stage."

The Japanese manufacturer has endured a difficult time under the new-for-2026 regulations as an engine supplier to Aston Martin.

The Silverstone-based team have generally been at the back of the field throughout the campaign, with the Honda power unit suffering from both a lack of power and reliability compared to their rivals.

Aston Martin sit only above F1 debutants Cadillac in the teams' standings, with Fernando Alonso scoring three points across two races, while Lance Stroll has yet to score.

At last weekend's Spanish Grand Prix, Stroll retired with brake issues, while Alonso managed to reach the chequered flag at his home event two laps down in P17.

Fukao has been with Honda since 2002, beginning with the development of engine and gearbox control systems before pivoting to Honda's involvement in MotoGP between 2009-2011.

Having then focused on the development of hybrid systems over the next three years, Fukao went back to F1, eventually becoming Deputy Leader of the F1 Project in 2017 and again in 2022 as Honda looked to return to the sport.

title: Was there any way for Norris to win in Madrid after the VSC?
excerpt:
Lance Stroll hit the brakes for Turn 20 and the pedal went to the floor.

Stroll’s stranded Aston Martin required a Virtual Safety Car to be cleared from the run-off area and Norris had just past pit exit to start Lap 14 when it was called, but Kimi Antonelli was there just in time to capitalise.

title: All the key moments from the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli claimed his eighth win of the season at the Spanish Grand Prix, the Mercedes driver extending his points lead in the title race as Formula 1 made its first visit to the Madring.

Although the Italian came out on top on the streets of Madrid, Lando Norris lost a potential victory due to an ill-timed Virtual Safety Car, while Lewis Hamilton's race was over almost before it started after brake problems.

Here are all the key moments from the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix…

Antonelli extends lead to 81 points after another victory

Kimi Antonelli put in yet another impressive display to become the first driver to take victory at the Madring, and record his eighth win of the season from 14 Grands Prix.

The Mercedes racer continues to march on in his quest for a maiden F1 title, with his margin over team mate George Russell now standing at 81 points.

Antonelli didn't really put a foot wrong all weekend, but was no match for Lando Norris' pace in the early stages of Sunday's race after starting second.

A short Virtual Safety Car deployment just as Antonelli headed to the pit entrance allowed him to take a cheap pit stop, as Norris missed his chance in the pivotal moment of the race.

Once Charles Leclerc's Ferrari made a late pit stop from the lead, Antonelli was back in front but acknowledged that Norris had been the quickest driver on the day.

“It’s good to win, but it doesn’t feel as good because I think Lando today deserved to win," said Antonelli.

In contrast, Russell was left to finish only P5 having made one extra stop than those ahead after being left compromised by starting in P6.

The Briton admitted post-race that any hopes of challenging Antonelli for the drivers' title had all but faded with nine Grands Prix still remaining.

"Realistically, I’m not in the fight for the drivers’ [title]," he said. "That just allows me to focus race by race and try to get some good results."

Antonelli insists Norris 'deserved to win' Spanish GP

Norris' Qualifying heroics undone by VSC

Just in case his victories in Hungary and the Netherlands weren’t enough to demonstrate the calibre of driver Lando Norris has become, the reigning World Champion executed what he confessed was “one of the best laps” of his F1 career in Qualifying.

With the exception of a small error at the final turn, the Briton mastered the latest addition to the calendar to edge out Mercedes’ Antonelli by 0.011s for his third pole position in four races.

With overtaking spots limited, it gave the McLaren driver a real chance of victory come race day.

And he got off to a confident start, rebuffing Antonelli's challenge when the lights went out, with the Italian making two small mistakes that enabled Norris to quickly build a lead at the front.

It was a somewhat cruel irony that soon after his engineer praised him for managing his tyres so well, the Virtual Safety Car was deployed and Norris missed the chance to take advantage, having already passed the pit entry when the alert came through.

McLaren still brought him in on his next tour to remain on the same strategy as Antonelli, both drivers having started on the medium compound, but by that time the VSC had ended and a painfully slow 7s stop dropped him down to P5.

He did manage to recover to the podium, which would normally be a result to celebrate against the likes of Mercedes, but the disappointment was palpable as Norris – and even the triumphant Antonelli – believed that he “deserved” the win.

Hamilton explains brake issues that caused Spanish GP DNF

Ferrari fail to capitalise on strong pace again

The Madring represented an opportunity for Ferrari to capitalise on the circuit's novelty and snatch a good result, especially after a disastrous home event at Monza.

Lewis Hamilton's head-on crash in the final hour of practice gave his mechanics a hefty repair job in order to make Qualifying, but that didn’t seem to dissuade the seven-time World Champion, as he went on to claim provisional pole with the first Q3 flying laps.

Ending up fourth in the final reckoning, directly ahead of team mate Charles Leclerc, there was still a possibility that a podium was on the cards, especially when Hamilton got a superb launch off the line.

Verstappen, who Hamilton had jumped, cut the chicane before eventually allowing the Ferrari driver back ahead, only for Hamilton to suffer a brake problem that sent him through several run-off areas and eventually forced his retirement.

It was a better day for Leclerc, who was likely left questioning what could have been had Ferrari’s hope of a Safety Car or red flag come to fruition. He did not pit under the VSC and thereby inherited the lead, but the lack of any further incidents left him with no choice but to finally pit after 48 laps on the hard tyres.

The gaps that had opened up between the frontrunners and the rest of the top 10 helped the Monegasque to come back out in P4, where he held off Mercedes’ Russell to bring home a respectable haul of points.

Best of the rest for Verstappen after giving positions up

Max Verstappen claimed P2 in Madrid, despite begrudgingly giving back places in the opening laps after tangling with Lewis Hamilton.

The Ferrari driver got ahead after lights out, with Verstappen cutting the first turn by driving off track to keep his P3 starting position.

The Dutchman said on the radio that Hamilton “almost shunted me”, and tried to resist Red Bull's instructions to give the place back to avoid a potential penalty, especially after he had since overtaken Antonelli for P2.

After giving in and allowing both Antonelli and Hamilton through, he quickly returned to the podium places after the Ferrari driver had a problem with his brakes.

Verstappen was also able to make the most of the VSC to limit positions lost during his pit stop, and eventually held off a charging Norris in the closing laps.

Ugochukwu takes F3 title in Madrid

Both F2 and F3 championships were in action at the Madring, with the latter concluding their season in the Spanish city.

Ugo Ugochukwu was up against Freddie Slater for the title, and it was the Campos Racing man who took the crown courtesy of a P2 finish in the final Feature Race.

Slater’s chances were dealt a blow when he was unable to score in the Sprint Race, before failing to finish the first Feature Race, meaning the pair entered the final race tied on points.

Eighth in the second Feature Race was not enough to deny his rival, Ugochukwu taking the title by 14 points in the end, with Tuukka Taponen also left celebrating after taking a maiden F3 victory on Sunday.

Over in F2, Dino Beganovic took a lights-to-flag victory in the Feature Race for DAMS Lucas Oil, as he led home Rodin Motorsport’s Alexander Dunne and Hitech’s Ritomo Miyata.

Championship leader Nikola Tsolov finished down the order, but his rival Rafael Camara could not capitalise, coming home P10 after a penalty to only narrowly reduce his deficit in the standings.

Tsolov leads by seven points, with those two set to resume their rivalry next time out in Baku.

Football stars out in force while Madrid welcomes tennis royalty to the paddock

There were plenty of famous faces from the world of sport on the Madring grid on Sunday, with Real Madrid giving a few players the day off to come and watch F1.

Their manager Jose Mourinho was also on the grid, and having beaten Rayo Vallecano 4-1 in La Liga action the previous evening, he was in an understandably good mood. As was Jude Bellingham, who scored in that match before using his Sunday off to catch up with some of his countrymen.

Vinicius Jnr was seen laughing and joking with Gabriel Bortoleto, while Real Madrid’s goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois towered over some of the drivers – at six foot seven, he is considerably taller than even the likes of Russell and Esteban Ocon.

Footballing legends David Beckham, Zinedine Zidane and Roberto Carlos were also in attendance, as was retired tennis star Rafael Nadal, who was spotted down at Ferrari.

title: What the teams said – Race day in Spain
excerpt:
Mercedes

Kimi Antonelli got a great start from P2, but when challenging for the lead cut the apex of the corner and was forced to cede position. His attempts to do so were messy and he briefly fell behind Verstappen until the Dutchman had to do the same thing. That left Antonelli second, a few seconds behind race leader Norris. But when the Italian got a cheap pit stop under the VSC, he became the de facto leader and from there he kept his race pretty clean to take his eighth win of the year.

As for George Russell, he had contact with Piastri at the start but was lucky to hold on to P6. The team opted to pit him under the VSC too, even though he started on the hards, and then did not think the mediums would last so pitted Russell a second time. That dropped him back again, and he finished fifth.

Kimi Antonelli, 1st

"It was great to get the victory today, but we know we were a little bit fortunate with the timing of the Virtual Safety Car. Lando (Norris) was in control at the front, but we were able to dive into the pits just as the Virtual Safety Car was deployed, make the cheap stop onto the Hard, get the net lead and run to the end. We probably didn’t deserve to win therefore but we will of course take it.

"We can also be happy with our pace today. We know we are still out of step with other teams in terms of upgrades, but we have been able to win the last two races at very different circuits. That is encouraging as we continue the season; we have a good position in the championships but we know there is still a very long way to go."

George Russell, 5th

"No matter what we had done with strategy today we would have finished P5. The Virtual Safety Car came at the worst point for everyone who had started on the Hard tyre like me, and the best point for those who had started on the Medium. Unfortunately, that is how racing goes sometimes but it is a little bit the story of my season so far! It was very difficult to overtake today but I’ve enjoyed driving the Madring overall this weekend.

"It is going to be an intense run to the end of the season. I’m looking forward to getting back to the factory, working with the team, and getting ready for the first of three triple-headers. My pace today, particularly on the Hard tyre, felt good so we can be encouraged by that as we head to Baku."

Toto Wolff, Head of Mercedes-Benz Motorsport

"We are pleased to have taken the first victory at the Madring; it has been another successful new event for F1 at a great location. Kimi drove well and, whilst the Virtual Safety Car played into his hands, he drove well to bring the car home at what has proved to be a very challenging circuit. To take another win at such a different track to Monza, having not brought a major update package to the car since Canada, is very encouraging.

"On George’s side, he was slightly unfortunate with the timing of the Virtual Safety Car. We started him on the Hard tyre, intending to go long, but we had to take the cheap stop under the Virtual Safety Car and to do something different if we were to try and beat Leclerc. The Ferrari stayed out and we switch George to the Medium but unfortunately it wasn’t the strongest tyre today. George reported early on that he was suffering so we went back to the Hard compound; ultimately whatever we had done we would have come home P5 today.

"We now have one week to get ready for Baku and the beginning of the first of three triple-headers. Extending our lead in the championships is good but we know there is still so much racing to come. It is going to be an intense run to the end of the season but we’re excited for that challenge."

Andrew Shovlin, Trackside Engineering Director

"That was a great result for Kimi and a really strong weekend for the team. We clearly benefited from the timing of the Virtual Safety Car, but credit goes to the drivers and everyone in the garage for being ready to react. The execution of both stops was excellent and that helped us take the win today.

"For Kimi, the decision to pit under the Virtual Safety Car was the one that ultimately put him in the net lead of the race. George's situation was a little more complicated. We had elected to do the opposite of Leclerc strategically because, when you're behind, you often need to try something different to create an opportunity. As the race unfolded, though, it became clear that the Hard tyre was performing better than we had expected and was the compound to be on. That said, if we had mirrored the Ferrari’s strategy, we would have still likely finished P5 with overtaking proving so difficult.

"Ultimately, the Virtual Safety Car arrived at the perfect moment for the cars that could switch onto the Hard tyre, and that's sometimes how racing goes. The important thing is that we've come away with a race win, a strong points haul, and strengthened our position in both championships.

"We'll regroup over the next few days and prepare for the run to the finish of the season. Nine races in 11 weeks is going to be a demanding stretch for everyone, but we've put ourselves in a good position in both title fights and we'll keep pushing right to the final Grand Prix."

title: Wolff explains decision on Russell's tyre strategy in Madrid
excerpt:
Mercedes boss Toto Wolff has backed the decision to bring George Russell into the pits twice during the Spanish Grand Prix after the strategy choice was questioned by the driver during the race.

The Briton made two stops during Sunday's event at the Madring on his way to a fifth-placed finish - firstly to change onto a new set of medium tyres during the Virtual Safety Car period and then again onto the hard tyre.

His team mate Kimi Antonelli executed a one-stop strategy, along with the majority of the other teams on the grid, and went on to win the race after Lando Norris lost out due to the timing of the VSC.

Russell was heard on the team radio asking his Race Engineer Marcus Dudley why they had decided to pit twice, saying he could have held off Norris who was behind him at that stage, before going on to finish fifth.

"He [Russell] said the tyres were not in a great shape, the mediums, we didn't think that they would go to the end," he said. "Then the pit opportunity was not to hang out and wait for a red [flag] but to change the tyres and get on with it."

The strategy appeared to have been discussed with Russell following the Grand Prix, who seemed content with the answer after the race whilst speaking to F1 TV.

"In the moment, I was questioning, but, you know, the hard tyre was the superior tyre," he acknowleged. "Maybe I could have stayed out with Leclerc, but I would have still finished behind him.

"Maybe I could have not pitted onto the hard again at the end. But everything I would have done brought us back to the same position, purely because you can’t overtake on this track, so that’s a shame."

In the same interview Russell appeared to rule himself out of winning the Drivers' Championship this season, after Antonelli's win saw him extend his standings lead to 81 points, but Wolff explained they'll work to help him with that mindset.

"You can have good races, bad races, good years and bad years, but we’re talking about a driver who has won everything he could have potentially won before," he said. "Karting championships, Formula 3 in his rookie year, Formula 2 in his rookie year, he went into Williams.

"We need to find out what it is for him to be able to unleash his potential."

title: Stella outlines the logic behind Norris’ ‘unlucky’ stop
excerpt:
McLaren Team Principal Andrea Stella has explained why McLaren opted to pit Lando Norris for fresh tyres just as the Virtual Safety Car period came to an end, admitting that “there was no option to retain the lead” of the Spanish Grand Prix.

With overtaking set to be a challenge at the Madring, Norris had already put himself in a strong position to chase down a potential third victory of the season as he topped Qualifying with a memorable last-gasp effort.

The Briton then succeeded in holding off Kimi Antonelli on the opening lap and gradually eked out a confident advantage over his rivals, managing his tyres until the Virtual Safety Car was deployed to recover Lance Stroll’s stricken Aston Martin.

While Antonelli and Max Verstappen could take advantage and box under the slowed racing conditions, Norris missed out on the opportunity and only headed into the pits as the VSC ended, where he suffered a 7s stop that dropped him to P5.

Despite his driver’s recovery to P3, Stella couldn’t hide the team’s frustration, as he told F1 TV: “Starting from pole position, leading the race and having incredible pace… this would’ve been a race won by many seconds, and we ended up in third position.

“The reality is that in racing, there are elements that you can control and some that you cannot control. The timing of the Virtual Safety Car was a couple of seconds too late – Lando had already passed the pit entry – and then he was a few seconds too early because then it was ending once he came in to pit.”

Asked to elaborate on the reasoning behind the call, Stella said: “The logic is that if you stay out, you stay out with used mediums [that are] already grained, and it means that at some stage you will pit behind the people that have already pitted on the hard tyres, so it’s going to be a similar race to [Charles] Leclerc.

“We would actually have pitted even earlier because the medium would finish earlier, so there was no option really to retain the lead.

“We needed to accept that the timing was incredibly unfortunate and, like I said, it’s a positive race overall.

“The elements that we could not control made a difference but those that we could control make us very optimistic for the future.”

McLaren have made steady gains throughout the season that culminated in Norris’ commanding victories in Hungary and the Netherlands, and this weekend further demonstrated their progress.

Max Verstappen, who only just kept him behind on the closing laps at the Madring, stated that the reigning World Champion was “faster than all of us”, while Antonelli believed that Norris “deserved to win”.

Stella concluded: “Just very unlucky, but I want to think that the positive message of a McLaren [that was] so competitive at a very different circuit layout to Zandvoort and Hungary is very encouraging for the future.

“We take it on the chin. Today we were too fast to win the race because had we been a little slower, we would’ve made it to the pits! We have a smile on our faces, we look forward to the rest of the season.”

title: Racing Bulls respond to Audi appeal as Yuki Tsunoda faces jeopardy
excerpt:
Racing Bulls boss Alan Permane is looking forward to a second trip to Paris after Audi appealed the stewards' decision not to penalise Yuki Tsunoda at Monza.

Racing Bulls team principal Alan Permane has addressed Audi's appeal against the stewards' decision not to punish Yuki Tsunoda for a start infringement at the Italian Grand Prix.

The German marque initially lodged its intention with the FIA after Tsunoda scored a point at Monza, with confirmation coming on media day for the Spanish Grand Prix at the Madring.

Following Charles Leclerc's red flag-triggering crash, Tsunoda lined up P14, but initially approached the wrong side of the grid before correcting his line and stopping in his allocated box.

His car was left at an angle towards the pit wall, prompting race director Rui Marques to abort the restart and order an additional formation lap. Under Article B5.9.4 of the sporting regulations, a driver deemed responsible for an extra formation lap must normally enter the pit lane and restart from there.

However, the stewards found Tsunoda had remained within his grid box and that the decision to run another formation lap was Marques' call.

Crucially, Racing Bulls had not been informed that Tsunoda was considered responsible, meaning it had no reason to instruct him to pit. The stewards therefore ruled that the extra lap resulted from the race director's assessment rather than being directly caused by Tsunoda.

Audi disagrees with that interpretation and stands to gain a point if the appeal succeeds. Gabriel Bortoleto finished P11, seven seconds behind Tsunoda, so overturning the decision would promote the Brazilian driver into P10 and hand him the final point.

"We raised a concern regarding the application of Article B5.9.4, which requires a driver who causes an extra formation lap to enter the pit lane and resume the race from there," Audi said in a statement. "The stewards issued a decision of No Further Action, and we have notified our intention to appeal."

Permane reacts to the appeal

Permane's response, meanwhile, came with a hint of humour. The Racing Bulls boss is set for another trip to Paris after the team's involvement in the FIA International Court of Appeal's recent hearing over the Monaco Grand Prix, where McLaren and Red Bull successfully appealed the reinstatement of Pierre Gasly's penalties.

That hearing took place in late August, with the decision published on 3 September during the Italian Grand Prix weekend.

"Well, it’s always nice to have a night out in Paris, first of all, or a second one in quick succession," Permane joked to media, including RacingNews365. "Look, we’ll go there, obviously, and defend the team and defend Yuki.

"I can’t really go into it more than that while it’s still an open case. Well, actually, it’s not even an open case yet because I don’t think it’s been… We haven’t even had a notification from the FIA to say.

"But I’m sure that will go ahead, and I guess, at some point in late October, we’ll head to Paris."

title: Former F1 driver issues apology after McLaren misunderstanding
excerpt:
Former Renault/Lotus and Haas F1 driver Romain Grosjean has taken to social media to apologise to McLaren Racing chief executive Zak Brown after misinterpreting remarks over the Spanish Grand Prix weekend.

Romain Grosjean has issued a public apology after misrepresenting comments made by McLaren Racing CEO Zak Brown about Oscar Piastri during the Spanish Grand Prix weekend.

The former Formula 1 driver was on commentary duty for French television channel Canal+ throughout the event in Madrid.

During his broadcast on Sunday, Grosjean referenced an interview Brown had given on F1TV's post-qualifying show the previous evening, describing the McLaren chief's remarks as leaving him speechless and characterising them as a pointed attack on Piastri's performance.

He went as far as to claim Brown had said Norris was a world champion and simply the better driver.

The comments spread rapidly on social media, becoming one of the talking points of race day.

Article continues below.

What Brown actually said about Piastri

The F1TV interview in question featured Brown alongside presenters Laura Winter, Grosjean himself, and former F1 drivers Juan Pablo Montoya and Jolyon Palmer.

When Winter asked for Brown's reaction to Lando Norris taking pole position, the McLaren chief was effusive in his praise for the reigning F1 drivers' champion.

"The whole lap was amazing and Lando's just getting better and better and better," Brown told them. "When you see a lap like that put down, you just go, 'he's a world champion'."

When Montoya then asked what Piastri, who had qualified seventh while Norris took pole, needed to do to close the gap in qualifying, Brown's response was measured rather than dismissive.

"I think a) you got Lando on his A-plus game, right? So I don't think there was anything left laptime-wise there. So he found that," Brown said.

"Oscar's been right there with him all weekend and just didn't get that same extra lap. We'll continue to look at it. He'll look at the data and probably do what we all did and go, 'wow, what a lap' as well."

Article continues below.

Grosjean apologises to Brown and McLaren

By Sunday evening, Grosjean had taken to social media to set the record straight and acknowledge that he had badly misjudged Brown's words.

"Today, I made a comment on Canal+ regarding Zak Brown's comments about Oscar Piastri during an interview yesterday on F1TV, which I was part of," Grosjean wrote.

"I completely misunderstood his words and want to apologise for that. I know how important it is to Zak and the entire McLaren team to respect their drivers and treat them fairly and equally."

Grosjean also took the opportunity to reflect on McLaren's race day in Madrid, where the team lost a likely victory after Norris was caught out by the timing of a virtual safety car period.

"McLaren had the fastest car today and were unlucky with the VSC," he added. "I'm sure both Lando and Oscar will have another chance to fight for the win in Baku."

title: Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend set for another major schedule change
excerpt:
The Baku City Circuit will host yet another unconventional weekend later this month after FIA Formula 2 confirmed a "supersized" round featuring two qualifying sessions and two feature races.

The F1 race itself was already moved from Sunday to Saturday to avoid clashing with Azerbaijan's Remembrance Day on 27 September, shifting the entire programme forward by a day.

Now F2's Round 12 will follow suit with a considerably expanded format, marking the only time this season the feeder series will stage more than one feature race in a single weekend.

As the sole support series at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, F2 will run a 45-minute free practice session on Thursday morning, followed by two consecutive 20-minute qualifying sessions on Thursday afternoon.

The sprint race and first feature race will take place on Friday, with a second feature race on Saturday morning ahead of the grand prix.

Championship leader Nikola Tsolov holds a slender seven-point advantage over Rafael Câmara heading into Baku, with Gabriele Minì a further 17 points adrift.

With two feature races each carrying the full 25-point haul for a win, plus fastest-lap points and pole position awards from both qualifying sessions, the expanded weekend could prove pivotal.

FIA Formula 2 CEO Bruno Michel said: "As Formula 2 is the only Support Event at the Azerbaijan Formula 1 Grand Prix, together with the promoters, we have opted for a supersized F2 race weekend, with one Free Practice, two Qualifying sessions, one Sprint Race and two Feature Races."

He added: "This is the only weekend where the timetable allows the additional sessions, which will increase the level of entertainment even further for the attending crowd and all our fans. The Baku City Circuit always provides us with amazing racing, so we're very pleased to make the 12th Round of our season pretty unique."

End-of-season uncertainty lingers

Michel confirmed that the final two rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi will revert to the standard format of one qualifying, one sprint race and one feature race.

However, there remains significant uncertainty over whether those events will go ahead at all.

The Qatar and Abu Dhabi Grands Prix remain officially on the 2026 F1 calendar, but contingency plans are in place should the regional security situation force cancellations.

Imola has been widely reported as a potential European replacement venue for a December season finale, though F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali has described it only as one option that is "not defined."

Whether F2 would also race at a potential Imola round is unclear, adding a further layer of unpredictability to a title battle that Baku could blow wide open.

title: Lando Norris Spanish heartbreak as Kimi Antonelli capitalises again - Spanish GP Winners and Losers
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli won the inaugural Madrid race from second on the grid, but the decisive moment of the Spanish Grand Prix was a virtual safety car that arrived two seconds too late for Lando Norris.

Norris had converted pole into the lead and controlled the opening stint until Lance Stroll stopped on Lap 15.

Race Control neutralised the race just after the McLaren had passed the pit entry, and the VSC ended as Norris finally came in, costing him around 20 seconds against rivals who stopped under delta conditions.

Antonelli took the win from Max Verstappen by 4.351s, with Norris third. Lewis Hamilton retired on Lap 7 with brake failure, and almost nobody overtook anyone.

So, who are RacingNews365's Spanish GP Winners and Losers? Find out below!

Winner - Antonelli takes control

Antonelli's eighth win of the campaign was not the most emphatic of his season, but it may prove the most valuable. He qualified 0.011s off Norris and never lost touch, then took the one strategic gift the race offered.

The 20-year-old leaves Madrid on 292 points, 81 clear of team-mate George Russell and 106 ahead of Norris. Mercedes now has 503 points to Ferrari's 358.

Antonelli has not needed to take risks to build that cushion; he has simply been in position every time a race has swung, and Madrid swung his way again.

© XPBimages

Loser - Norris loses one he had won

Norris did everything asked of him and lost 15 points of value to a rule. McLaren team principal Andrea Stella conceded that some elements of racing cannot be controlled, noting the VSC came a couple of seconds too late and then ended a few seconds too early.

Norris himself argued that a rule should not decide a race, and that he was the only driver on the grid denied the cheaper stop.

At a circuit where recovery was near impossible, third was all that remained. He is 106 adrift with the season running out, which makes this the sort of afternoon a title challenge does not survive twice.

© XPBimages

Winner - Verstappen overachieves again

Second place in a Red Bull that has no business being there was voted as the drive of the weekend by F1 fans. Verstappen qualified third, 0.140s off pole, and then defended against Norris to the line.

Context matters: under the FIA's ADUO rules for 2026, Red Bull Powertrains was designated the benchmark internal combustion engine, locking the team out of the upgrade concessions handed to rivals.

Red Bull has openly disputed the methodology, saying its own data does not match the governing body's. Verstappen is sixth in the standings on 145 points, which flatters nobody except the car. Madrid was further brilliance from the 28-year-old.

© Red Bull Content Pool

Loser - Hamilton's title bid ends

Hamilton qualified fourth, within two tenths of pole, and was out of the race by Lap 7. He described the brake failure as sudden: the pedal stepping down into Turn 5, the car refusing to slow, a brush with the barrier, then the pedal going long a few corners later.

He said he did not know where it had come from, and Ferrari has not yet identified the root component.

He was reportedly told to nurse the car home rather than stop on track, protecting Leclerc's long opening stint on hards. Hamilton stays on 191 points, third, now 101 behind with the calendar shrinking.

© XPBimages

Winner - Colapinto shines again

Ninth in qualifying, seventh at the flag, and six points that move Franco Colapinto to 27 for the season.

On a track where positions barely changed hands, the Argentine kept Oscar Piastri's McLaren behind him by 1.558s and looked very competitive. Team-mate Pierre Gasly was 12th and a lap down, which sharpens the comparison considerably. Alpine sits sixth on 68 points.

Colapinto's weekend was built in qualifying, exactly as Madrid demanded, and that is the clearest evidence yet that the 23-year-old has settled into the seat.

© XPBimages

Loser - The Madring's damaging debut

The circuit's problem is structural, not circumstantial.

Drivers reported that narrow sections and badly configured corner entries left essentially nowhere to pass, with the curved braking zone into the Turn 5 chicane singled out: Oliver Bearman pointed out that braking on a curve removes the alternate line needed to go up the inside.

Verstappen went further, arguing the design should never force drivers to steer and brake at once, and offered to redo the braking zones himself. Piastri rated only Monaco harder for overtaking.

No FIA or organiser review has been confirmed, and whether anything changes before 2027 is the question Madrid now has to answer.

© XPBimages

title: Maximilian Günther signs multi-year deal in Envision Formula E switch
excerpt:
Maximilian Günther will race for Envision from the upcoming season after signing a multi-year contract, the Formula E squad has confirmed.

The seven-time race winner arrives as Envision steps up its preparations for the Gen4 era, which formally begins with pre-season testing at the Circuit del Jarama on 16-20 November.

Günther brings eight seasons of Formula E experience to the team. Born in Oberstdorf, the 29-year-old started karting at the age of 10 before moving into single-seaters in 2011.

He finished runner-up in the FIA Formula 3 European Championship in 2016 and third overall the following year, before graduating to Formula 2. His first taste of Formula E came at the 2018 rookie test in Marrakesh, which earned him a reserve role and then a race seat at GEOX Dragon for Season 5.

The breakthrough followed in his second season, when he won the 2020 Santiago E-Prix at 22 years old to become the youngest race winner in the championship's history, a record that stood until Taylor Barnard's victory in the recent season finale last month.

Günther has often shown strong pace wherever he has held a seat, although that was difficult last campaign with DS Penske. He announced his exit from the outfit following the London finale, where there were already reports of a move to Envision. If given a competitive package, the German can deliver for Envision.

"We are thrilled to announce Max as our newest driver at Paysafe Envision Formula E Team," said team principal Sylvain Filippi.

"Season 13 is going to be an important year for all teams; learning the Gen4 car as well as a new sporting format, which is going to put an even bigger focus on outright pace and speed.

"Max has proven how capable he is at delivering qualifying laps when it matters, as well as podium finishes and race wins.

"We're incredibly excited to start working with him and hit the ground running at pre-season testing in November."

Günther hails Envision's 'exceptional quality'

Günther's Formula E career has seen him race for GEOX, BMW, Nissan, Maserati and DS Penske. Representing big brands has never been an issue, of which Envision is very much one having featured in the series since the very beginning as Virgin Racing.

Envision is opting for an entirely new driver pairing for the start of Gen4, with Günther's team-mate yet to be announced. No matter who he partners, Günther could very easily prove to be a highly underrated signing.

"I'm very happy to become a Paysafe Envision Formula E driver for the Gen4 era and I really look forward to our future together," said Günther.

"The team has a very successful history in Formula E and exceptional quality throughout the organisation. Our aim is to combine our strengths and achieve great success, competing at the very top.

"I truly believe we have all the ingredients to build something really special together. What convinced me about the project was the great environment, the high ambition of the team, the mindset and, of course, the excellent technical package together with Jaguar.

"I'm proud to become part of the team and have a fantastic feeling about our future."

title: Toto Wolff reveals Kimi Antonelli anguish with 'cool' comparison
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has described Kimi Antonelli using the simile "cool as a cucumber" following his victory at the Spanish Grand Prix.

The Mercedes driver was not the quickest driver at the Madring, with that honour going to Lando Norris, but took advantage of a fortuitously timed virtual safety car to clinch his eighth win of the F1 season from second on the grid.

In doing so, the 20-year-old increased his lead over team-mate George Russell in the drivers' standings to 81 points, with eight or nine rounds to go.

However, Antonelli — and not for the first time this year — stressed out Wolff on the pit wall with his flat-out nature, despite comfortably controlling the latter stages of the 57-lap race in Madrid.

When appraising his driver's performance and his tendency to push the limit even when leading, the Mercedes team principal told Sky Sports F1: "I think he's cool - sometimes an inch too cool!

"When he brushes the wall five laps from the end and comes on the radio, 'check the car,' you're like, 'really, again, white lines, walls,' but maybe that's how he keeps himself in the zone.

"Almost his youth helps him a lot because he's 20. He could stay in this sport for 20 years with so many opportunities. He's so above all of our expectations and his own. He's just going with the flow.

"I think there is also a genetic factor. You are born cool as a cucumber, or you're not."

Wolff - 'You see junior drivers crumbling in Formula 2'

Wolff, expanding on his remarks, highlighted how Antonelli differs from other young drivers with his ability to absorb pressure without wilting from the expectations of the moment.

With a healthy advantage in the F1 drivers' championship, the Italian only needs to consistently rack up points over the remainder of the schedule.

However, he shows no signs of letting up and is perfectly content to continue in his current gear.

"You can see this in junior formula or karting - taking pressure easier," Wolff added. He's taken this to another level.

"We are talking about Formula 1. You see junior drivers crumbling in Formula 2.

"He's just doing his thing. We told him, 'This is a race where we need to bring it home, need to score points whether it's P2 or P5, we don't care, just drive it home'.

"He does that and goes fast."

title: Ferrari launch 'thorough' investigation into Lewis Hamilton brake failure
excerpt:
It's not the first time Ferrari has had brake issues with its cars this season.

Ferrari has promised a full investigation into the brake system failure that forced Lewis Hamilton out of the Spanish Grand Prix.

Hamilton had qualified fourth at the Madring, but retired after just six laps, ending his streak - and the last in F1 this season - of scoring points in every race.

The seven-time F1 champion confirmed after the race that the pedal dropped a step under braking for Turn 5, leaving him carrying too much speed and brushing a barrier. He explained that the pedal then returned to normal before going long again a few corners later.

Although Ferrari attempted to resolve the problem from the pit wall, the fault reappeared, forcing him out of the race.

"At this stage, we don't yet know the exact cause of the brake system issue that forced him to retire," said Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur, speaking to the media after the race, including RacingNews365. "But we will investigate it thoroughly.

"The pedal was long. We tried to fix it from the pit wall, and then it happened again."

A long pedal is typically traced to a hydraulic pressure loss. Ferrari has had recurring brake-feel issues this year, although it remains unclear whether the Madring failure is linked.

[Article continues below]

Long game for Leclerc

Leclerc salvaged the weekend for Ferrari with fourth, 29.116s behind race winner Kimi Antonelli and just 0.713s clear of George Russell.

The Monégasque ran an extremely long opening stint on the hard tyre as Ferrari gambled on a stoppage that never came.

"Like a few other teams, we split the strategy, starting one car on the soft compound and the other on the hard," Vasseur explained.

"With Charles, we were leading the group that started on the hard tyre, and he drove a very strong first stint, pushing for almost 50 laps while maintaining good pace throughout.

"We knew there was a reasonable chance of a safety car or a red flag, so we decided to extend the stint and keep that opportunity open.

"A red flag could have put us in a position to fight for the win, while a late safety car could have given us a shot at third. In the end neither happened, but I think it was absolutely worth trying and Charles delivered a very solid performance."

Hamilton stays third in the drivers' standings on 191 points, with Leclerc fifth on 167 heading to the next grand prix in Azerbaijan on Saturday, September 26.

title: Honda announce major F1 shake-up amid miserable first Aston Martin season
excerpt:
Honda Racing Corporation has made a change in the leadership of its F1 project midway through its debut campaign with Aston Martin, which has fallen far short of expectations.

Honda Racing Corporation will replace the leader of its F1 power unit programme from 1 October, installing Yoichiro Fukao as 'large project leader' in place of Tetsushi Kakuda, who oversaw the development that powered Max Verstappen to four consecutive drivers' titles with Red Bull.

The change comes 14 rounds into a wretched debut campaign alongside Aston Martin, with the works partnership languishing 10th and last in the constructors' championship on just three points, all scored by Fernando Alonso.

The two-time F1 drivers' champion sits 19th in the drivers' standings, with a best finish of ninth at the Dutch Grand Prix. Lance Stroll, meanwhile, is yet to trouble the scorers.

Honda framed the transition as a planned succession designed to transfer technical expertise to the next generation of engineers, and to establish a development framework ahead of further regulatory changes expected from 2027.

Fukao, currently serving as Honda's deputy F1 project leader and head of its software division, has been with the F1 programme since 2002, working on engine and gearbox control systems before a spell in MotoGP and mass-production hybrid development. He returned to the F1 project in 2014 and has held increasingly senior roles since.

A difficult start, and a modest upgrade

Honda's RA626H power unit suffered severe vibration issues from the outset of the season, with concerns at one stage that the problem could cause nerve damage to drivers. Neither Aston Martin car finished any of the first three races due to reliability failures linked to the Honda unit.

A "Spec 2" upgrade introduced at Zandvoort addressed the worst of the vibration problems and delivered what Honda's trackside general manager Shintaro Orihara called a step forward.

"We have observed a step forward in terms of performance," Orihara said. "We have confirmed on dyno, so that was a positive thing we found."

Yet Orihara was also candid about the scale of the deficit, estimating the upgrade was worth between 0.05 and 0.1 seconds per lap, a figure Alonso essentially dismissed as irrelevant given the chasm to the front.

Aston Martin remained around two seconds off the pace at the Hungarian Grand Prix, even after a comprehensive 16-element aerodynamic upgrade to the AMR26 that included a reworked floor, diffuser, front wing, sidepod inlets and rear wing.

The chassis work has been widely acknowledged as a significant step, but without a competitive power unit underneath it, the gains have counted for little in the standings.

From Red Bull highs to Aston Martin lows

Honda's pedigree in the current turbo-hybrid era is beyond question. The Japanese manufacturer powered Verstappen to four straight drivers' titles and Red Bull to consecutive constructors' championships in 2022 and 2023, amassing more than 70 grand prix victories across its partnership with the Milton Keynes team.

That success, though, came after Honda's painful three-year stint with McLaren from 2015 to 2017, a period defined by chronic unreliability, power deficits and, eventually, a very public divorce.

There are uncomfortable parallels to those early McLaren struggles in the current Aston Martin project, though Honda has been careful to manage expectations.

Before the season, Honda Racing Corporation president Koji Watanabe defined success in 2026 as ensuring the new works partnership functions as one integrated team, with championship ambitions positioned as a medium- to long-term goal.

Orihara has confirmed there will be no further major power unit updates this season. "This is the only major update for this year," he said. "The major update will be in 2027."

title: George Russell demands major change after 'sore head' pain
excerpt:
George Russell was left with a "sore head" following the Spanish Grand Prix and is demanding changes to the Madring.

George Russell has demanded changes to the Madring circuit layout after a "not pleasant" experience in the Spanish Grand Prix left him with a "sore head."

The new 22-turn circuit in the Spanish capital was limited in its overtaking opportunities, with the only realistic place to make a move being at Turns 5 and 6 at the end of the longest straight on the circuit.

However, the curved arrival into the braking zone leads into a fast left-right-left chicane which does not create overtaking opportunities for drivers with no big stop as cars clatter over the kerbs.

Following a fifth place finish which saw his points deficit to race-winner Kimi Antonelli balloon to 81 points, Russell was keen for changes to be made for the 2027 event.

"They need to do something, they need to make a change," Russell told media, including RacingNews365 of the track layout.

"Because every circuit needs to have an overtaking opportunity after a bit of a straight, and this one has a tight chicane and the corners that are a real challenge, but it is not pleasant.

"After 60 laps smashing those kerbs, my head was a bit sore at the end."

The article continues below.

© XPBimages

Russell reflects on "far better" Spanish GP

As for his race, Russell laboured to a fifth-place finish, having started on the hard tyres and running long, losing a further 15 points to team-mate Antonelli.

"The hard tyre was by far the superior tyre, and it would have been a big gamble to stay out on the medium, and I thought I had nothing to lose in the end," he said.

"I think I would have ended up where I ended up anyway, so it is a bit of a shame; it is a very tough track to overtake, which I guess was a bit annoying for everyone.

"The performance was far better than the result, and I think the pace was really strong, among the strongest of everybody out there, so I take those positives, but this was Monaco-esque in terms of qualifying [being important]."

title: Lando Norris reveals 'rejected' F1 driver talks after race-defining moment
excerpt:
Lando Norris has revealed F1 drivers have held discussions over rules regarding the use of the virtual safety car after he lost Spanish Grand Prix victory due to its deployment.

After Lance Stroll stopped the Aston Martin on track, the VSC was deployed at the Madring, but leader Norris had crucially passed the pit-entry in the McLaren, whilst Kimi Antonelli was six seconds behind in the Mercedes, and was able to duck into to pits, as did Max Verstappen.

This meant Antonelli and Verstappen were able to complete their pit-stops under VSC conditions and save race-time, whilst Norris was forced to do a full lap at VSC speeds, before then pitting just as the VSC was lifted.

He then carried out a stop at full racing speed, meaning he dropped down to fourth on the road, but in a net third as Charles Leclerc was out front goal-hanging for a further safety car or virtual safety car for a cheap stop.

This did not come as Antonelli won from Verstappen and Norris, with the world champion feeling that the way the race was won and lost was "not the way you should lose."

"I'm past the pit lane, so I need to speak to the team, but it's not a guessing game, so I was just unlucky," Norris told Sky Sports F1.

"I was the only one on the whole grid that didn't get a pit stop, so I lose 20 seconds on the whole grid. This is out of my control. It's out of their control. It's a rule. It shouldn't define a race.

"A race should be won by the guy who can put in the best performance, who maybe takes a risk by going long in a pit stop, going long in a stint, and maybe you get a safety car later on, and things can help because you know that's one of the big factors.

"But for everyone to get a safety car for a VSC pit loss, and [for me] to get nothing, it's just unfair, but it's happened in the past.

"Others have won from it. I've probably won from it in the past, and I don't think many people have lost a race win over it.

"It's frustrating. I don't feel like it's the way you should lose. We've spoken about it in the past in the drivers' briefing, saying they should leave it out at least a full lap, so it's equal for everyone.

"I was the only one who lost out, and I lost out about 20 seconds of race time, and that's not how it should be."

The article continues below.

Ongoing debate around safety cars

The current F1 rules allow drivers to pit under safety cars or virtual safety cars for strategic reasons, and tyres are also allowed to be changed under red flags.

It has long been a topic of debate about closing the loophole, but we want to know what your thoughts are.

title: Max Verstappen doubles down on Lewis Hamilton claim after radio fury
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has stood by his stance on the first-lap near-miss with Lewis Hamilton at the Spanish Grand Prix, insisting he had little choice but to run off the track through Turns 1 and 2.

The Red Bull driver initially moved into second behind pole-sitter Lando Norris, but only after Hamilton's attempt to gain ground through the opening complex left Verstappen taking to the escape road.

Verstappen emerged ahead, only to be instructed to give the position back after race control noted him for leaving the track and gaining an advantage.

Clearly unhappy with Red Bull's instruction, and questioning why he should surrender the place, believing Hamilton had forced him off the circuit, he eventually complied, which dropped the Dutchman from second to fourth, with Kimi Antonelli also promoted back ahead of him.

Verstappen's frustration before and after that decision sparked an angry exchange over Red Bull's team radio.

"Mate, what the f*** are you guys talking about? He would've shunted it," he fumed to race engineer Gianpiero Lambiase. "Like, what are you guys talking about? If I just stay on the track, I am out of the race."

To add insult to injury, Hamilton's race ended just a few laps later with a brake failure, and Antonelli subsequently went on to win, helped by Norris' misfortune with the Virtual Safety Car.

Hamilton, for his part, subsequently played down the incident, saying it was "pretty good racing" and, when asked about Verstappen's complaints, simply replied: "Nothing to do with me."

It was particularly costly for the 28-year-old, given the difficulty of overtaking at the tight Madring, with the four-time F1 drivers' champion consigned to a race behind Antonelli from there, holding Norris at bay in the closing stages.

"Maximised the result," he told media, including RacingNews365. "Probably a bit lucky, of course, with the unlucky situation for Lando, because I didn’t have the pace of Kimi, and I definitely did not have the pace of Lando.

"We’re here on the podium, and I think that’s great, but we still lack a little bit to really fight for the win; because it might have looked a little bit like we were in a fight for the win, but that was more because Kimi was getting held up by Charles.

"Because as soon as he had clean air, he just drove away from me again, and I was busy with Lando behind me. But around here, if you drive a little bit in the middle, then you can’t pass."

Verstappen: 'I would have definitely had contact'

The Red Bull driver was then asked whether retaining his position after the opening-lap incident could have allowed him to challenge Antonelli for victory.

Verstappen disagreed, reiterating his belief that staying on the circuit would have resulted in contact with Hamilton and potentially ended his race before it had properly begun.

"I would have had damage at the start if I would have stayed on track, so then the win was also not on," Verstappen replied.

"It’s as simple as that. I just did my own thing in Turn 1, but Lewis went for a move on the first two and bottomed out on the kerb, so he just jumped back onto the track, and that’s why I had to go off the road.

"If I would have stayed there, I would have definitely had contact. So, then my race could have potentially been over in Turn 2, and that’s why I think, where we are now, I’m happy to be."

title: Oscar Piastri concedes 'going too far' after rare FIA warning
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri has conceded that it was "easy to go too far" after receiving a rare warning from the FIA in the Spanish Grand Prix.

The McLaren driver was handed a black and white flag for exceeding track limits during the race, in which he was carrying damage on the front-wing after first corner contact with George Russell's Mercedes.

As the damage continued to impact the handling and performance of the MCL40, Piastri picked up a rare black and white flag for driving standards as he was deemed to be cutting corners and exceeding track limits.

Reflecting after his eighth-placed finish, his worst since 11th in Canada, Piastri explained how the contact with Russell happened and why he was pushing the boundaries, and picked up the rare flag warning.

"It was just a tough afternoon from literally the start," reflected Piastri to media, including RacingNews365, after his 11th consecutive grand prix without a podium finish.

"From then on, the rest of the race was very compromised, obviously with some of the damage and the track position mainly.

"I was alongside, and he just kept squeezing me to the wall, and then I hit the brakes and kind of avoided him. But amongst all that, he hit the brakes as well. Everyone hit the brakes, and we kind of got stuck together and everything.

"I was just expecting a bit more space, and obviously between a car and a wall, you can't make any more space, so that was tricky.

"On a track like this, you're always searching for a bit of clean air in the high-speed corners, and with no kerb or wall on the inside of some of the corners, it's very easy to just go a little bit too far."

The article continues below.

Piastri's "good race"

Despite finishing eighth, 1m:30s behind team-mate Lando Norris and the last car on the lead lap, Piastri felt he had enjoyed a good race "in clean air" but being stucked in a "train" had cost him after emerging from the pits behind cars, including Franco Colapinto's Alpine, who finished seventh.

"I think the pace and clean air on the hard was pretty good, but we were trying to make up the pit loss of the VSC to the guys who pitted, and once they got the loss back, I was stuck again, so that was painful," said Piastri.

"Then when we pitted onto the medium, we pitted into a four-car train, and that wasn't great, and the medium tyre was just awful.

"It was good for [one lap], and then it was pretty terrible, so a lot of things to try and fix."

title: Liam Lawson reveals 'a lot of risk' behind rare Madring overtake
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has conceded he had to "take a lot of risk" to complete one of the few overtakes of the inaugural Spanish Grand Prix at the Madring.

The Red Bull driver finished sixth in Madrid, 86.746s behind race winner Andrea Kimi Antonelli, after starting on the hard tyre and running a long first stint.

A virtual safety car worked against him, but Lawson said his weekend had previously been compromised by qualifying. The New Zealander started from eighth on the grid.

Lawson's move on Franco Colapinto, following a change of tyres, was one of the rare passes on a circuit that drew heavy criticism across the weekend from all the drivers.

Organisers have since signalled they are open to layout changes for future editions.

[Article continues below]

'Easy for it to go wrong' - Lawson

Speaking after the race, Lawson confirmed he had also been compromised by a virtual safety car, called on lap 15 after the Aston Martin of Lance Stroll had sustained a brake issue, forcing him to park his car in a run-off area.

"We started on the hard, and that sort of forced us to go a bit longer," said Lawson, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365.

"The VSC wasn't ideal, but considering where we started, I think the damage for us was really done in qualifying, so it's a good result.

"But it's so hard to overtake. I had to take a lot of risk with Franco to make that pass, and I barely, honestly, made the corner without doing track limits. It's just hard with the way this track layout is, but it's fun to qualify on, just difficult to race on.

"Looking at other categories as well, it's obviously quite mental. In F2, F3, there were quite a lot of crashes. It's just easy for it to go wrong."
